title: The Myth of the Productive Morning
paragraphs: Every few months, an article arrives in my inbox announcing the secret habits of successful people. Almost invariably, the first habit is getting up early. Chief executives, we are told, rise at half past four, run ten kilometres and answer messages before the rest of us have found our slippers. I have read perhaps fifty of these pieces, and I have drawn only one conclusion from them: that I am doomed.

I am, by nature, a night person. My mind does not truly switch on until mid-morning, and it reaches its best around ten at night. For years I treated this as a defect to be corrected. I bought an alarm clock that rang at six, then another that rang at a quarter past, and I spent a long stretch of my twenties tired and ashamed, convinced that the problem was a lack of discipline.

Eventually I discovered that the problem was not mine alone. Researchers who study sleep use the term chronotype to describe the natural tendency to be alert at certain times of day. This tendency varies widely between individuals, and it is partly inherited. Forcing a night person to work at dawn is not so much a test of character as an attempt to make a left-handed person write with the right hand: possible, but needlessly costly.

It is not hard to see why the early-bird legend persists. Society was organised around the early riser long before anyone studied chronotypes. Schools start at seven, offices at eight and meetings at nine, while evening work is regarded, a little suspiciously, as a sign of disorganisation. People who thrive in the early hours therefore enjoy an advantage that has nothing to do with merit, and those who do not are quietly penalised for it.

Nor is the evidence for the miracle of mornings as strong as the articles imply. Successful people do get up early, but so do many who are not successful, and it is hard to know which causes which. A company director may rise at five because she has the means to take a nap in the afternoon, or because a household manager handles the children. Copying her alarm clock without her circumstances is unlikely to produce her results.

What, then, should be done? I suggest the following modest experiment. For two weeks, record not the hours you sleep but the hours in which you feel most capable, and try to schedule your most demanding task for that time. Employers can help by allowing flexible hours wherever the work permits. Not every job can be moved, of course; a baker cannot postpone the bread. But many jobs can, and the gain in energy is often considerable.

I am not arguing that early risers are fools or frauds. Some people are genuinely at their best at dawn, and I envy their quiet hours. My claim is simply that there is no single best schedule, and that a habit which suits one body may be harmful to another. The sensible question is not when the most successful people wake up, but when you do your best work. Mine, as it happens, begins at about ten at night, and I wrote this column then.

title: Why Octopuses Are Not Little Humans
paragraphs: An octopus in an aquarium will, given a jar with a screw lid, unscrew it from the inside to reach the food. It will recognise individual keepers, squirt water at those it dislikes and, on occasion, escape through a gap barely larger than its eye. Stories of this kind have made octopuses celebrities. Yet the temptation to see them as clever humans in a tentacled suit misses what is most interesting about them: they are intelligent in a way that is entirely their own.

Consider the family tree. The last ancestor that octopuses share with humans was a simple, worm-like creature that lived more than half a billion years ago. Since then, the two lineages have evolved complex brains separately, which makes the octopus the nearest thing we have to an intelligence of independent origin. If we ever want to know what minds can be like, the octopus is perhaps the best case study on our planet.

The body plan is startlingly different from ours. An octopus has roughly half a billion neurons, a number often compared with that of a dog, but the majority are found in its arms rather than in its central brain. Each arm can, to a remarkable degree, taste, touch and make local decisions. A severed arm may continue to react to stimuli for a time. It is as though the animal were a committee, with a chairman at the centre and a great deal of independent staff.

Other features remind us how unlike us they are. They have three hearts and blue blood, and most species live only one or two years. They are generally solitary, and do not raise their young: a mother typically guards her eggs until they hatch and then dies. This means that octopuses cannot learn from parents or elders, which sets them apart from most intelligent animals, whose skills are taught as much as inherited.

Why, then, are they so clever? Scientists offer several hypotheses. A soft-bodied animal without a shell is exposed to predators and must rely on quick thinking, whereas a flexible body with hundreds of suckers demands extensive control. Complex environments such as reefs may also reward curiosity, as hiding places must be found and prey must be outwitted. These explanations are plausible, but they remain educated guesses.

The ethical implications are difficult to ignore. If octopuses can feel pain and solve problems, then how we keep and catch them matters. Some countries have already recognised them in animal welfare laws, and a number of researchers argue that regulations should be extended. Others reply that it is hard to measure suffering in a creature whose nervous system works so differently from ours, and that caution should not be confused with certainty.

Perhaps the best lesson is one of humility. We tend to measure other minds by how much they resemble ours, and then to be surprised when something very different proves clever. The octopus invites us to imagine intelligence on other terms: distributed, curious, short-lived and solitary. It has, after all, been solving problems in the dark for a very long time, and it never needed our approval.

title: The Bus Driver Who Writes Poems
paragraphs: Ignacio Paredes starts his shift at five in the morning, when the avenues of Montevideo are still half dark. He drives route 121 for a little over nine hours, a circuit that crosses the city from the port to a southern suburb. Between stops, in the brief pauses at traffic lights, he glances at a small notebook wedged beside the steering wheel. In it, written in pencil, are the lines of poems that he has not yet finished.

Paredes, fifty-six, has been a driver for twenty-eight years. He began writing, he says, in the second decade, when he noticed that nobody described the city he saw from his seat. 'People write about the sea, the football, the old cafés,' he told me during a break. 'Nobody writes about the woman who gets on at the hospital at six and falls asleep before the second stop.' Those were the people he wanted to put on paper.

His poems are short, plain and often funny. One describes a schoolboy who practises a speech aloud to the window. Another, titled 'Ticket', imagines the journeys taken by a single coin passing from hand to hand. He avoids ornate language, partly from conviction and partly from habit. 'If a passenger cannot understand the poem in the time between two stops,' he says, 'it is not finished.'

For years, nobody except his family read them. Then a regular passenger, a literature teacher, noticed the notebook and asked to see it. She photographed some pages, with his permission, and posted them online. Within a month, a small publisher had written to ask whether he would consider a book. 'I thought it was a joke,' Paredes recalls. 'I said I would think about it. I thought about it for two weeks, and I could not sleep.'

The collection appeared last year, with a print run of one thousand copies, and sold out in four months. The cover shows a bus seen from behind, its rear window glowing yellow in the rain. Paredes has since been invited to give readings in bookshops and cultural centres, where he arrives in his uniform, partly because he has no other jacket he likes and partly, he admits, because he is nervous without it.

Not everything about the sudden attention has been comfortable. A newspaper called him 'the poet driver', a label he dislikes. 'I am a driver, and I am a person who writes,' he says. 'The two jobs do not need to introduce themselves.' He also worries that success might change how he looks at things. 'If I start to see people as material,' he says, 'I shall have to stop.'

On the day we met, Paredes finished his shift at two in the afternoon, parked the bus in the depot and sat for a moment in the empty driver's seat. He opened the notebook and wrote a single line, then crossed it out. 'Tomorrow,' he said, smiling. Outside, the city was beginning its slow afternoon, and somewhere on route 121, I felt, a poem was waiting at a traffic light.

title: The Quiet Revolution of Audiobooks
paragraphs: Ask a literature lover whether listening to a book counts as reading, and prepare for an argument. Some will say that the ear is simply another door into the same house. Others will hold that something essential is lost when the eye is excused from its work. After years of listening to stories while I cook, walk and travel, I find that I belong to neither camp, and that the question itself is more revealing than any answer.

The defenders of print have a case. Reading with the eyes allows control: one can pause, re-read a sentence, skip forward or let a paragraph sit before moving on. A narrator, however good, sets a tempo that the listener must follow, and her voice may colour the text with an interpretation that the author never intended. Complicated arguments, in particular, are often easier to grasp on the page, where the structure is visible.

Yet the oldest literature in the world was heard before it was read. Epic poems were recited long before anyone wrote them down, and for most of history stories were shared aloud, at fires, in markets and at bedsides. What we call silent reading is a relatively recent habit. Seen in this light, the audiobook is not a degradation of literature but a return to one of its original forms.

It is also a more democratic form. People with visual impairments or dyslexia have found in audio a way into books that print had made difficult. Commuters who cannot hold a paperback on a crowded bus can nevertheless follow a novel, and parents who barely have a free hour can fold a story into household chores. For many, the choice is not between listening and reading; it is between listening and not reading at all.

I would add that the quality of the experience depends greatly on the narrator. A good performer can reveal the humour in a sentence that the eye might have skipped, or give each character a distinct voice. A poor one can ruin a masterpiece. This is a feature, not a flaw, because it ties the audiobook to the traditions of theatre and storytelling, which have always depended on the skill of the person speaking.

None of this makes the printed page obsolete. Different formats suit different books and different moods, and a sensible reader will use both. I tend to read dense non-fiction on paper and to listen to novels, particularly long ones with a strong voice. The difference is one of habit, not of principle, and I suspect many readers feel the same way.

So does an audiobook count as reading? I am inclined to say that the better question is what a book does to us. If a story has changed how we see a person or a place, the means by which it entered our heads seems a minor detail. The revolution, in the end, is a quiet one: it has not replaced books, but it has taught us that they were never confined to paper.

title: Provisional
focus: Narrative tenses and free indirect style
paragraphs: Mateo Cifuentes had taught at the university in Barcelona for six years on contracts that lasted, at most, nine months. Each June he cleared his shelf of books into three boxes, in case the renewal did not arrive; each September, relieved, he unpacked them again. His flat had the temporary air of a place inhabited by someone who expects, at any moment, to be asked to leave. The only item that had remained in permanent position was a cactus, which flourished out of what seemed to be spite.

That autumn, the department announced one permanent position. Mateo, who had not applied for anything in three years, applied at once, and was astonished to find himself invited to an interview. He used the week before it to rehearse replies in front of the cactus. Do you see yourself in this institution in ten years? Of course. Where else would he be, unless the boxes spoke up?

The committee consisted of four people, three of whom he knew well. Dr Valls, the chair, had been his supervisor; she smiled at him the way one smiles at a favourite nephew who has come to borrow money. Mateo spoke fluently about his research, about his students, about a reading group he had started on his own time. The questions were friendly. Only afterwards did he realise that nobody had asked about the future.

The result arrived by email two weeks later. The position had been given to a candidate from Lisbon, a woman with more publications and, according to the polite phrasing of the message, 'a profile that complements the department's international strategy'. Mateo read the sentence three times. It did not seem to say that he was bad. It simply said that he was not what they were missing, which was worse, because it left nothing to improve.

He told nobody for a day. On the second evening he called his mother in Bogotá, who answered after the first ring, as though she had been holding the telephone for hours. She did not offer advice. She told him instead about the neighbour's dog, the price of oranges at the market and the rain that had been falling since Tuesday. He listened to all of it, and felt, for the first time that week, that something was ordinary.

The following Monday, he did something unusual. He took the three boxes from under the bed, and instead of putting them away he carried them, one by one, to the bookshelf and unpacked them completely. The books looked odd in their places, as though they were guests who had been told to stay. It took the whole afternoon. When he had finished, the room seemed smaller, and for the first time in years it seemed like his own.

His contract was renewed in the spring, again for nine months. Mateo signed without ceremony. In June, the boxes stayed where they were, and the cactus, in its pot by the window, put out a single orange flower that nobody had expected, least of all the cactus.
glossary: presidente(a) de un comité o departamento

title: Coastal Erosion Assessment: Summary
paragraphs: ## 1. Scope of the assessment

This summary presents the results of a technical assessment of shoreline change along a twelve-kilometre stretch of coast in the municipality of Playa Larga, on Mexico's Pacific coast. The assessment compared aerial images taken at five-year intervals over the past thirty years, and was complemented by field measurements and interviews with fishermen and residents. Its purpose is to inform a planning decision on where new construction should be permitted.
## 2. Observed change

Over the thirty-year period, the shoreline retreated by an average of twenty-two metres. The rate of retreat has not been uniform: it accelerated during the last decade, with an average annual loss of just over one metre, compared with roughly half a metre per year before. In the southern sector, where a river mouth was dredged in the nineteen-nineties, losses reached forty metres in some locations.

Three factors are considered to contribute. First, the construction of a breakwater at the port has altered the movement of sand along the coast, and tends to deprive the beaches to the south of material. Second, sea level has risen gradually, increasing the reach of storm waves. Third, the removal of dune vegetation for building has reduced the natural protection of the shore. The relative weight of each factor cannot be established with certainty.

Interviews with fishermen largely support these findings. Several reported that the beach where their boats were once drawn up has narrowed so much that they now moor them in a different location, and two described losing storage sheds to storm waves in the past five years. Residents of older houses, by contrast, tended to attribute the changes to natural cycles and were less inclined to believe that human intervention played a significant role.
## 3. Exposure

Approximately 340 buildings lie within fifty metres of the present shoreline, of which 190 are permanent dwellings and the remainder are hotels, restaurants and fishing facilities. If the current rate of retreat continues, a substantial proportion of these buildings would be exposed to regular flooding within twenty years. Insurance coverage is limited, and the majority of the affected households have not been informed of the risk.
## 4. Options

Three broad options were considered. The first, defending the coast with hard structures such as sea walls, would protect existing buildings but is expensive and tends to accelerate erosion on neighbouring beaches. The second, restoring the dunes and limiting new construction near the shore, is cheaper and more sustainable, but delivers results slowly. The third, organised relocation of the most exposed properties, is the most effective in the long term and the most difficult socially.
## 5. Recommendation

The assessment recommends a combination of the second and third options. No new building permits should be issued within a hundred metres of the shoreline, and dune restoration should begin in the most degraded sectors. A voluntary relocation programme, with fair compensation and the participation of residents, should be designed within two years. These measures should be reviewed at five-year intervals in the light of new data.

title: The Unlisted Landfill
paragraphs: For eight years, residents of a hillside neighbourhood near Belo Horizonte have complained of a smell. It arrives in the evening, they say, a sour, heavy odour that makes it impossible to open the windows. In the past two years, some have begun to notice something else: a grey film on the surface of a stream where their children once played. The municipality insists that nothing is wrong. Its own records, however, tell a more complicated story.

Our investigation began with a single document. Obtained through a freedom-of-information request, it is a municipal inspection report from three years ago, which refers to 'an area of deposit not included in the official register of landfills'. The site, a former quarry on the edge of the neighbourhood, appears in no public list. Yet satellite images, reviewed by an independent geographer, show lorries entering it almost every day from 2021 until last year.

We spoke to three drivers who had worked on the site. All asked for anonymity, fearing that they would lose their licences. They described unloading mixed waste, including, according to two of them, containers marked as industrial. 'Nobody asked what was inside,' said one. 'They paid by the load, in cash, and signed nothing.' A company named in connection with the site did not respond to questions sent on four occasions.

A laboratory commissioned by this newspaper tested water from the stream. The results, reviewed by an environmental chemist who was not involved in the testing, showed concentrations of certain metals above the limits for drinking water, though not far above them. The chemist cautioned that a single sample could not prove the source of the contamination. 'It is consistent with leakage,' he said, 'but also with other explanations. It needs a proper study.'

The municipality's response illustrates the difficulty. A spokesperson said that the site had been 'under review' for some time, but could not explain why it had not been closed or listed. She added that the municipal budget for environmental inspection had been cut by a third last year. This may well be true; it is also true that no inspector has visited the site in two years, according to the council's own log.

Residents are not waiting. A group of about sixty families has formed an association and is collecting signatures for a petition. 'We are not experts,' said Cláudia Ribeiro, a schoolteacher who lives two hundred metres from the quarry. 'But we know what our own stream looked like ten years ago.' The association has asked the state prosecutor's office to open an inquiry, and it is expected to respond within weeks.

What this case shows is less a scandal of one site than a weakness in oversight. A place that is not listed cannot be inspected, and a place that is not inspected can continue to operate. Until the register is complete, and until those responsible for filling it have the means to do so, the smell on that hillside is likely to be only the part of the problem that people can notice.
glossary: solicitud de acceso a la información pública

questions.q: The municipality admitted that the site was a problem from the start.

The company had very few customers
The drivers were government inspectors
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: el pago en efectivo, por carga y sin firmar documentos sugiere que el vertido se ocultaba intencionalmente.

questions.q: How does the reporter treat the laboratory results?
options: Cautiously, noting their limits
As unimportant and unreliable
As final proof of guilt
questions.explain_es: Actitud: los presenta con reservas: son 'consistent with leakage' pero también con otras explicaciones; 'It needs a proper study'.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To announce the closure of the site
To describe the smell in more detail
To draw a wider conclusion about oversight
questions.explain_es: Propósito: el caso muestra 'a weakness in oversight': un lugar sin registro no puede inspeccionarse.

questions.q: How does the report begin?
options: With a quotation from the prosecutor
With residents' complaints and a contradiction with official records
With a list of dangerous chemicals
questions.explain_es: Estructura: abre con las quejas de los vecinos y anuncia que los registros oficiales cuentan una historia 'more complicated'.

questions.q: In 'a spokesperson said that the site had been under review', 'under review' means…
options: being cleaned
being examined
being sold
questions.explain_es: 'Under review' significa en revisión, en proceso de examen.

title: Translation and Betrayal
paragraphs: The Italian saying traduttore, traditore, 'translator, traitor', is a perfect example of what it describes. In English, it loses its sound: the two Italian words differ by only a few letters and chime together like a bell, while their English equivalents clatter apart. The proverb thus demonstrates its own point: anyone who tries to carry a text from one language into another must lose something along the way.

What exactly is lost? Not necessarily the information. Any competent translator can explain what a sentence says. What is more fragile is everything surrounding the information: the rhythm of the phrase, the associations of a word, the humour that depends on a pun, the formality that is built into a pronoun. Spanish distinguishes between tú and usted, and English, which has only you, must either ignore that distinction or find some other way to signal it.

This is why the greatest translators are often described as writers in their own right. They do not simply replace words; they make hundreds of small decisions, each of which is a judgement about what matters most in a given sentence. Should the translator preserve the strangeness of the original, even at the cost of fluency, or should he make it read as though it had been written in the new language? There is no neutral answer. Either choice sacrifices something.

There is a further complication. Words do not always map onto each other neatly. The Portuguese word saudade is often called untranslatable, a mixture of longing, nostalgia and affection for something absent. Yet the claim is exaggerated. English speakers feel the emotion perfectly well; they merely lack a single word for it. The gap lies in the vocabulary, not in the experience, and good translation works by finding other ways, a sentence, an image, a footnote, to bridge it.

Machine translation has changed the landscape considerably. Software can now produce readable versions of most texts in seconds, and for many practical purposes, travel signs, emails, instructions, the results are perfectly adequate. But a literary text is a different matter. A machine does not know why an author has repeated a word three times in a paragraph, or why a joke should be allowed to fall flat. It follows patterns, and literature is, among other things, the art of departing from them.

I would not want to give the impression that translators are doomed to fail. On the contrary, translation is one of the means by which cultures have always learned from one another. Without it, most of us would never have read the Russian novelists, the Greek tragedians or the Latin American writers who changed our idea of what a novel could be. The loss is real, but it is almost always smaller than the gain.

Perhaps the proverb should be amended. A translator is not a traitor, but a negotiator, someone who knows that every agreement involves concessions and tries to make them wisely. Anyone who reads a translated book is therefore in the position of a person at a signing ceremony: grateful for the peace, and aware that somewhere in the small print a few things have been given up.

questions.q: The author says that translators always lose all the information in a text.
questions.explain_es: Escribe: 'Not necessarily the information. Any competent translator can explain what a sentence says'. Lo frágil es el ritmo, la humor y las asociaciones.

questions.q: The author argues that saudade describes an emotion English speakers can feel.
questions.explain_es: Dice que 'English speakers feel the emotion perfectly well; they merely lack a single word for it'.

questions.q: What does the author suggest about literary translation by machines?
options: It is already better than human translation
It is useful only for poetry
It struggles with deliberate departures from patterns
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: la literatura es 'the art of departing from' patrones, y la máquina sigue patrones y no sabe por qué se repite una palabra.

questions.q: What is the author's attitude to the proverb 'translator, traitor'?
options: Fully in agreement with it
Scornful of its origin
Appreciative, but ready to revise it
questions.explain_es: Actitud: reconoce su acierto, pero propone enmendarlo: el traductor es 'a negotiator'.

questions.q: Why does the author open with the Italian proverb?
options: To introduce a story about an Italian translator
To illustrate the problem of translation at once
To criticise the Italian language
questions.explain_es: Propósito: el proverbio pierde su sonido en inglés y por eso demuestra su propio argumento.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph relate to the first?
options: It returns to the proverb and revises it
It repeats the same idea without change
It introduces a different language
questions.explain_es: Estructura: el ensayo empieza y cierra con el proverbio, que en la conclusión se reformula con la metáfora del negociador.

questions.q: In 'Yet the claim is exaggerated', 'exaggerated' means…
options: carefully proved
widely accepted
made to seem greater than it is
questions.explain_es: 'Exaggerated' es exagerado: la afirmación presenta algo como mayor de lo que realmente es.

title: A Calculator for the Essay
paragraphs: When calculators first appeared in classrooms, many teachers were alarmed. If children could press a button to find an answer, they asked, what would become of arithmetic? Decades later, the calculator has not destroyed mathematics. It has changed what schools ask of students: less long division, more problem-solving. I recall this debate whenever I hear colleagues declare that writing tools based on artificial intelligence will be the end of the essay.

I should say at once that the comparison is imperfect. A calculator performs an operation that has one correct answer; a writing tool produces a text whose quality is a matter of judgement. A student who copies a generated essay has not shortened a task so much as skipped it, and has learned very little. Teachers are right to be concerned about that. The question is what to do next.

Banning the tools seems to me the least promising response. Detection programs are unreliable, and they tend to accuse the wrong people, particularly those who write in a second language and whose clean, careful prose resembles that of a machine. A school that punishes such students on the basis of a faulty program does more harm than any amount of cheating could do. Prohibition also pushes the practice underground, where nobody can discuss it.

A better response, I think, is to change the assignment. If the aim is to see how a student thinks, then ask for the thinking. Ask students to write in class, to discuss their draft aloud with the teacher or to explain why they chose a particular argument. Ask them, even, to use the tool deliberately and to criticise what it produces: to find the weak reasoning, the invented references and the sentence that sounds impressive and says nothing.

That last exercise is, in my experience, remarkably effective. Students who have to find the errors in a machine's essay quickly discover how many errors there are, and begin to read their own writing with a sharper eye. In a workshop I observed in Mexico City, teenagers spent forty minutes marking up a generated text with red pen, and several remarked, with some surprise, that it was harder than writing their own.

Naturally, there are risks. Some students will use the tools to avoid effort, as some have always used shortcuts of every kind. Access is also unequal: pupils with fast internet and a personal computer are better placed to benefit than those who share a phone with three siblings. If we adopt these tools, the school has a responsibility to make sure that the advantage does not become another form of inequality.

Writing has never been merely a product. It is a way of finding out what one thinks, and no tool can do that on our behalf. For that very reason, the machine need not frighten us. If we teach students to treat it as an assistant whose work must be checked, we may produce readers more demanding, and writers more honest, than any generation before. The calculator, after all, did not end mathematics; it made us ask what mathematics is for.

questions.q: The author believes that banning writing tools is the most promising response.
questions.explain_es: Escribe que 'Banning the tools seems to me the least promising response'.

questions.q: The author mentions that detection programs can accuse students wrongly.
questions.explain_es: Dice que son poco fiables y 'tend to accuse the wrong people', sobre todo a quienes escriben en una segunda lengua.

questions.q: What does the author imply about students who write in a second language?
options: They never use writing tools
Their careful prose may be mistaken for machine text
They are more likely to cheat than others
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: su prosa limpia y cuidadosa 'resembles that of a machine', por lo que los detectores pueden acusarlos injustamente.

questions.q: How does the author's attitude to AI tools in education differ from that of some colleagues?
options: He is more optimistic, but not naive
He is more fearful of them
He is indifferent to them
questions.explain_es: Actitud: no cree que sean 'the end of the essay'; propone adaptarse, aunque reconoce los riesgos y la desigualdad de acceso.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the calculator comparison in the first paragraph?
options: To show that mathematics is no longer important
To prove that calculators are better than computers
To suggest that fears about new tools can be exaggerated
questions.explain_es: Propósito: la historia de la calculadora muestra que la herramienta cambió lo que la escuela pide, sin destruir la matemática; el autor aclara luego que la analogía es imperfecta.

questions.q: What function does the paragraph on risks serve?
options: It introduces the author's main thesis
It repeats the first paragraph
It acknowledges drawbacks before concluding
questions.explain_es: Estructura: el párrafo de los riesgos (esfuerzo evitado y acceso desigual) reconoce los inconvenientes antes de la conclusión.

questions.q: In 'a sentence that sounds impressive and says nothing', 'impressive' means…
options: very short
admirable at first hearing
hard to read
questions.explain_es: 'Impressive' es impresionante: la frase suena admirable, aunque no diga nada.
